evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it: as a checked reference sheet of K-ary regrets, worst cases and curvatures, yes, the formulas are all right and reproducible in 0.5 s. As research: nothing here is new (the author says so), and the note cites nothing, so a reader cannot place it against Savage 1971 / Gneiting & Raftery 2007 (Bregman representation, which gives every regret and curvature here as the divergence and Hessian of the entropy), Bickel 2007 (the direct log/quadratic/spherical comparison), Selten 1998, or the bounded-payment optimal-scoring-rule work that already compares incentive per unit range. The repo-specific motivation (decentralised ML verifiers) is asserted, not argued. The rare-class conclusion (bounded scores pay O(rho^2) for a dropped class) is standard and correct, but the log comparison is floor-dependent. 2.
evidence.domain: Reviewer: a decision theorist working on proper scoring rules. Method compared against the Savage/Gneiting-Raftery representation (score from a convex entropy G, regret = Bregman divergence of G, local regret = half the Hessian quadratic form). Departures: none in the formulas, which match my derivations; the quasi-concavity argument for the spherical vertex minimum is right. A reviewer would reject: the wrong explanation of the sqrt(K) mechanism (s.3), the floor-dependent log number used as a headline contrast, mixing raw-unit regrets across bounded and unbounded scores in E4, and the absence of any literature for a comparison (incentive per payment range) that is an established normalisation. 2.

defects.what: The whitepaper cites no prior work at all. Every result is textbook or near-textbook: regret as the Bregman divergence of the score's entropy (Savage 1971; Gneiting & Raftery 2007, JASA), Brier regret ||r-p||^2 and log regret KL, comparisons of quadratic, spherical and log rules (Bickel 2007, Decision Analysis; Selten 1998 on the quadratic score), pseudospherical families (Jose, Nau & Winkler 2008), and the comparison of incentive per unit of bounded payment range, which is the normalisation used in the scoring-rule optimisation literature (e.g. Li, Hartline, Shan & Wu, 'Optimization of scoring rules', EC 2022; Neyman, Noarov & Weinberg 2021). 'Not new theory' is said honestly, but a reader cannot tell which of the vertex worst-case formulas or the sqrt(K) ratio is a known result and which is this note's.

E4's log regret for dropping a rare class (0.151 at rho=0.01) is set by the arbitrary floor r_0=1e-9, not by the log score: the same drop costs 0.289 at a 1e-15 floor and is infinite at 0 (leading term rho*ln(rho/eps)). The paper reports it as a fixed number beside bounded-score regrets in raw units (Brier range 2, spherical 1, log unbounded), so the '1e-4 vs 0.15' contrast in the README and s.4 is a units-and-floor comparison. The Brier value has the closed form rho^2 K/(K-1), which the paper does not give.

Zero-boundary behaviour of the log score is untested: three of six seeded mutations survive the 6 tests - kl returning 0 instead of inf for a zero report on a supported class (model.py:49), exp_loss including zero-mass classes (0*inf -> nan, model.py:33), and log_loss returning 0 for r_y=0 (model.py:29). Every test draws interior points with rng.expovariate, so the claims 'log is infinite' and 'log is not blind to a dropped class' rest on code no test exercises. The closed forms and curvature formulas themselves are well guarded (3 of 3 mutants caught).

Section 3 explains the sqrt(K) gap as 'spherical using its whole range while Brier uses [0,2] only at vertices'. Both scores reach their extremes only on the boundary; the actual mechanism is the 1/||p|| factor in the spherical curvature (per-range ratio = (||d_perp||^2/||d||^2)/||p||, maximal at uniform where ||p||=1/sqrt(K)).
Section 4 says spherical per-range curvature is '1.75-2.2' over a sentence that runs from rho=0.5; E2 gives 1.386 at rho=0.5, so the range is 1.39-2.24.

'verified against finite differences to 0.1%' while the test asserts only |ratio-1|<0.005 (assertAlmostEqual places=2), i.e. 0.5%; my check gives 3e-4, so the claim is true but not what the test verifies. E1's 'log max inf' is a literal string in run.py:6, not computed.
No input validation: functions accept any vector (max_regret_* assume the simplex silently), pair_shift can produce negative mass without complaint, curv_log divides by zero for p_j=0.

verdict: The mathematics is right. Independent brute force over the simplex reproduces the Brier and spherical worst-case regrets exactly (uniform(5): 0.800 and 0.2472; rho=0.001: 1.2475 and 0.4985), the closed-form regrets agree with direct expectation to 1e-15, the sqrt(K) per-range ratio at a uniform truth holds exactly and is a true upper bound over 200k random truths, and run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte. It does not meet the bar, on verification: three of six seeded mutants survive, all in the log score's zero handling (kl, log_loss, exp_loss), which the paper's 'log is not blind to a dropped class' rests on. As research it is a correct reference note, not a contribution: it cites no prior work at all for results that are textbook (Savage 1971, Gneiting & Raftery 2007, Bickel 2007), its headline log number in E4 (0.151) is set by an arbitrary 1e-9 floor (0.289 at 1e-15), and its stated reason for the sqrt(K) gap is not the actual mechanism (the 1/||p|| factor). Correctness, completeness, craft and claims 3; verification, fitness and domain 2.
